page.title: Best Laser Engraver for Beginners (2026): Software, Bed Size and Real Cut Tests
page.h1: Best laser engraver for beginners: xTool M2 10W, and when a LightBurn machine fits better
page.desc: The xTool M2 10W is the easiest first laser engraver, from $499, but it runs only xTool Studio. The Creality Falcon A1, A1C and A1 Pro are compared on LightBurn support, bed size and reviewer cut tests.
page.answer: Short answer. The best laser engraver for beginners is the xTool M2 10W: a Class 1 enclosed machine with two cameras and a 426 × 320 mm bed, from $499. The catch: it runs only in xTool Studio, not LightBurn. If you want LightBurn, the Creality Falcon A1 10W ($549) runs it.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Bed vs the A1C: the M2's 426 × 320 mm bed is 136,320 mm², 6.1 times the Falcon A1C's 150 × 150 mm (22,500 mm²), for 1.9 times the price ($499 ÷ $269 = 1.86). The A1C makes sense only when your projects fit a 5.9 in square: coasters, tags, keychains.
  • Bed vs the Falcon A1: 136,320 ÷ 116,205 mm² (381 × 305) = 1.17, so the M2 gives 17% more bed for $50 less ($549 − $499) at the makers' stores.
  • Bed vs the A1 Pro: 358 × 268 mm = 95,944 mm², 70% of the M2's bed (95,944 ÷ 136,320) for $600 more ($1,099 − $499).
  • 10W vs 20W cutting speed: xTool's M2 FAQ rates 3 mm basswood at 8 mm/s with the 10W module and 15 mm/s with the 20W, both at 100% power in one pass: 15 ÷ 8 = 1.9 times faster. The 10W's 3 mm black acrylic cut is a 2-pass job.
  • Noise: an enclosure doesn't make a laser quiet. 3DPrint.com measured the Falcon A1 at 75 dB average and 80 dB peak with its air pump running, and CGMagazine also reported about 75 dB. Plan for a garage or spare room, and vent smoke outdoors or through a purifier.

Which app each machine runs, and what that locks in

xTool's M2 FAQ (updated Nov 5, 2026) says "xTool M2 is not compatible with LightBurn or XCS". Its only software is xTool Studio for Windows and macOS. LightBurn's own xTool device table agrees: it marks the M2 "Unsupported" and lists the xTool S1, F1 and P2S as supported. Without a computer connected, the M2 "can only process the task last executed on the device". Its hardware is M2-only too. The FAQ says processing modules from other xTool machines don't fit and that "Accessories not listed here are not compatible with xTool M2."

For most first-time owners that's a plus. With one app, the M2 takes photos, aligns the design, focuses and measures the material thickness by itself (xTool FAQ). The lock-in starts to matter if you want to follow LightBurn tutorials, work on Linux, or run a second laser from one program.

Creality's Falcons go the other way. LightBurn staff member Aaron.F says the Falcon A1 and A1 Pro run "modified GRBL" firmware. He traced an air-assist shutoff on both machines to a Creality firmware bug, and Creality's debug firmware 1.0.7 fixed it for two users. CNX Software's Jean-Luc Aufranc lists LightBurn and LaserGRBL for the A1 Pro on Windows and macOS, with Linux only through LightBurn. The A1C is less settled. On 2026-09-30, LightBurn developer Jeremy Lee wrote "we haven't updated the driver to support the A1C fully yet". One user found that Home and jog worked over Wi-Fi but Frame did not, while USB with LightBurn's Falcon A1 device profile worked. LightBurn's Aaron.F recommends the GRBL device type for now.

Dealectric has no partner program for these brands; every link goes to the maker's own store.

Not recommended

The Falcon A1 Pro, if you'd buy it as a first machine for one-pass thick cuts. In CNX Software's test, a 10 mm basswood cut at 85% power and 600 mm/min took 7 passes in a 10 min 15 s engrave-and-cut job, and the piece still had to be pried out by hand. At $1,099 it costs $600 more than the M2 for 70% of the M2's bed. The 20W laser buys speed on thin stock, not single-pass cuts through thick wood.
